parsed.summary: The formal statements say four things about R_k(3), defined as the least n such that every k-colouring of the edges of K_n has a monochromatic triangle: (i) R_k(3)^{1/k} → ∞; (ii) the explicit bound R_k(3) ≥ ((1/(6e^{38}))·k^{1/3}/log k)^k for all k ≥ 2, together with (i); (iii) for every ε > 0 and all large k, (1/4−ε)·k log k ≤ log R_k(3) ≤ (1+ε)·k log k; (iv) log R_k(3) = Θ(k log k). The definitions are faithful. The main caveat is that the lower coefficient in (iii) is 1/4, weaker than the paper's stated exponent 1/3 − o(1).

glossary.plain: A k-colouring C of E(K_n) in which no colour class contains a triangle (each label graph is 3-clique-free).
Every k-colouring of E(K_n) contains a monochromatic triangle.
R_k(3) = least n with the arrow property; sInf ∅ = 0 would apply only if the set were empty.
glossary.note: For k ≥ 1 the set is nonempty by Ramsey's theorem, so sInf is the true minimum. For k = 0 the value is 2 (vacuous labellings), which is irrelevant to the asymptotic and k ≥ 2 statements.

lean_claims.plain: For every ε > 0, for all sufficiently large k: (1/4−ε)·k log k ≤ log R_k(3) ≤ (1+ε)·k log k.
log R_k(3) = Θ(k log k) as k → ∞.

paper_claims.plain: There exists an absolute c > 0 with R_k(3) ≥ (c·k^{1/3}/log k)^k for all k ≥ 2.

coverage.why: Gives the explicit constant c = 1/(6e^{38}) rather than just existence of some c.
Lower coefficient is 1/4 − ε instead of 1/3 − o(1); the upper coefficient 1 + ε matches.
log R_k(3) = Θ(k log k) is the same statement as R_k(3) = k^{Θ(k)}.

flags.explanation: The paper states the lower bound k^{(1/3−o(1))k}. The Lean statement only proves the lower coefficient 1/4 − ε, which is strictly weaker. The full 1/3 claim follows from (3) but is not stated formally.
flags.probe_idea: ∀ ε > 0, ∀ᶠ k in atTop, (1/3 - ε) * k * Real.log k ≤ Real.log (triangleRamseyNumber k)

flags.explanation: For k = 0 the definition gives R = 2 because labellings into Fin 0 are vacuous. The value is only nonstandard at k = 0 and does not affect any target statement, since all of them are asymptotic or restricted to k ≥ 2.
